title: Forgive, or fight back?
hookLine: in the forest, Draupadi argues for might and Yudhishthira for kshama, forgiveness, and Prahlada's old answer weighs both
carry: kshama is strength, but dharma reads the hour
tomorrow: they were cheated. why keep the promise?

lines: A COUPLE ARGUES IN THE FOREST.
WHY IS YOUR ANGER NOT BLAZING?
BOTH OF THEM GET THE FLOOR.
cards: An evening in the forest, and a married couple is having a real argument. Draupadi looks at her husband in his bark clothes, sleeping on the ground, and she can't stand it. You were a king, she says.
Your brothers are suffering. How is your anger not blazing? Yudhishthira doesn't storm out.
He answers her, at length. And she answers back. The epic doesn't cut the scene short or tell us who won.
It gives both of them the floor.

teach.b: Draupadi doesn't argue from feeling alone. She brings a story.

Long ago, she says, the demon king Bali asked his grandfather Prahlada, the same Prahlada whose verdict Vidura told in the hall: which is better, forgiveness or might? Prahlada answered: neither one, always.

Someone who forgives everything is treated with contempt, even by his own servants. Someone who never forgives makes enemies of everyone. There's a time for each, and wisdom is knowing which time it is.

teach.h: DRAUPADI: NOW IS THE TIME FOR MIGHT.
teach.b: Now, says Draupadi, is the time for might. Yudhishthira answers with a different picture. Anger, he says, is the root of destruction; an angry person can't tell what should be said from what shouldn't.
Forgiveness holds the world together. He calls it the strength of the strong. The word he praises is kshama: forgiveness, patience under wrong, and old Hindu lists of the marks of dharma include it.
So who is right? Here's the teaching the scene leaves you with.
Kshama is a real strength, not a weakness. But Prahlada adds the word that keeps it honest: time.
Dharma isn't one rule for every moment; it reads the hour. Is the person sorry? Is this the first time?
Would forgiving now protect anyone, or only let the harm go on? Draupadi isn't the hothead, and Yudhishthira isn't the saint. Both quote their tradition.
That's why, in many Hindu homes, 'forgive' and 'stand up for yourself' can both be dharma. The wisdom is knowing which hour it is.

how: Teachers and commentators return to this forest debate between Draupadi and Yudhishthira when discussing anger, kshama (forgiveness) and right action, and Prahlada's answer to Bali, a time for each, is retold on its own as well.

o: the court where kings judge right and wrong
a hermit's vow to give up anger for good
the forest where the exiled couple argue it out

games.q: the forest argument — tap the pairs.
p: now is the time for might
forgiveness is the strength of the strong

s: Prahlada said forgiveness is always best
he said neither forgiveness nor might is right every time; wisdom knows which time it is.
Draupadi supported her argument with an old story
she told of Bali asking his grandfather Prahlada about forgiveness and might.
in Hindu teaching, kshama, forgiveness, is a kind of weakness
Yudhishthira calls it the strength of the strong; Prahlada only warns that its time must be read.

games.q: a classmate tore down your posters, then came and said sorry. with Prahlada's answer in mind, what fits?
o: forgive him, and speak up if it happens again.
never forgive; forgivers get walked on.
forgive everything, every time, no matter what.
games.why: Prahlada: neither one always. kshama is strength, but dharma reads the hour, and a real first apology is a time to forgive.

practice: Bring to mind one wrong someone did you, a medium one, not the biggest. Breathe in with Draupadi's question: is this a time for strength? Breathe out with Yudhishthira's: what would carrying this anger do to me?
Then ask Prahlada's: what does this hour call for? If you pray, ask for kshama, and for the wisdom to know its time; if not, just let the three questions sit.

wordCard.voice: Vana. The forest of exile, where Draupadi argues for might and Yudhishthira for kshama, and both are heard.

orig.note: Sanskrit kshama: forgiveness, patience under wrong.

carryVoice: Your line: kshama is strength, but dharma reads the hour. Prahlada's answer was that each has its time. Tomorrow: they were cheated, so why keep the promise? That's day seven hundred seventy-nine.
